Section 147(1)(b)(i) which clearly refers to "damage to any property of a third party" and not damage
to the property of the 'insured' himself. And the limit of liability fixed for damage to property of a
third party is Rupees six thousand only as pointed out earlier. That is why even the Claims Tribunal
constituted under Section 165 is invested with jurisdiction to adjudicate upon claims for
compensation in respect of accidents involving death of or bodily injury to persons arising out of the
use of motor vehicles, or damage to any property of a third party so arising, or both. Here also it is

restricted to damage to third-party property and not the property of the insured."
The restrictions relating to appeal in terms of Section 173 (2) does not apply to own damage cases.
A plea has been taken about the desirability of purposive construction.
"Golden Rule" of interpretation of statutes is that statutes are to be interpreted
according to grammatical and ordinary sense of the word in grammatical or liberal
meaning unmindful of consequence of such interpretation. It was the predominant
method of reading statutes. More often than not, such grammatical and literal
interpretation leads to unjust results which the Legislature never intended.

args.question: We represent National Insurance Co. The deceased's family claims compensation for a death caused by our insured's truck, whose driver had no valid driving licence. What precedents support our defence, and what authorities cut against us?

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving a motor vehicle without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy, absolving the insurer of direct liability to indemnify the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had no driving licence at all on the date of accident — directly on point with our facts where the truck driver had no valid licence.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest authority for establishing that the licence defect is a 'fundamental breach' — not a minor or inconsequential deviation. The tribunal expressly held the insurer 'not liable to pay the compensation' and 'absolved from its liability' to the insured, though it ordered pay-and-recover for the third party.
supporting.quote: Hence, it is held that as rightly argued by the learned counsel for the respondent No.2 the respondent No.1 has breached the fundamental condition of the policy by allowing the driver who has no driving licence to drive the vehicle. ... the respondent No.2 is not liable to pay the compensation and he is absolved from its liability.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: The insurer bears the initial burden of proving the breach under Section 149(2). Once proved, the insurer must still satisfy the third-party award but is entitled to recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: This Full Bench decision clarifies the burden of proof framework: the insurer must prove the breach (no valid licence) and the insured's negligence in permitting the unlicensed driver. Our case aligns because we can prove the driver had no licence.
supporting.why_it_matters: Provides the complete legal framework: (a) burden on insurer to prove breach, (b) even after proving breach, pay third party, (c) recover from insured. It also cites Swaran Singh's principles on what constitutes a fundamental breach.
supporting.quote: Even if there is any violation or breach of condition of a policy, the insurer has to discharge the initial burden of proving the grounds taken under Section 149(2) of the Act. In spite of that, the insurer has to indemnify the amount and can recover the same from the insured.

supporting.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
supporting.principle: The Swaran Singh principles apply exclusively to third-party risks and have no application to own-damage claims. A fake licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
supporting.fact_alignment: While this case is about fake licences and own-damage claims, it confirms that the Swaran Singh framework (which limits insurer defences) is confined to third-party claims — which our case is. It also confirms that where the licence is fundamentally invalid, the insurer's position is stronger.
supporting.why_it_matters: This Supreme Court judgment is the only one in the corpus that expressly favours the insurer. It clarifies that the 'pay and recover' principle applies to third-party claims (which is our case) and that the insurer's right to recover is well-established.
supporting.quote: In view of the above analysis the following situations emerge: 1. The decision in Swaran Singh's case (supra) has no application to cases other than third party risks. ... 3. In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver holds only an LMV licence but drives a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions, and the insurer is entitled to pay and recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: Our case involves a truck (goods carriage/transport vehicle). If the driver had no licence at all (not merely the wrong class), this case is less directly on point, but it supports the principle that driving without the proper authorisation is a breach.
supporting.why_it_matters: Demonstrates the insurer successfully proving breach through examination of an RTO official (RW.1) and documentary evidence. Provides a template for how to discharge the burden of proof.
supporting.quote: By examining R.W.1 and by adducing evidence on the driving licence particulars of 3rd Respondent, the Insurance Company has discharged the burden cast upon it in establishing that the driver did not have a valid driving licence to drive a transport vehicle and that there was violation of policy conditions.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar W/O Late ...
supporting.principle: Where a driving licence has lapsed and is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, the renewal takes effect from the date of renewal, not retrospectively — so the driver had no valid licence on the accident date.
supporting.fact_alignment: While our case involves no licence at all (not an expired one), this case supports the broader principle that absence of a valid licence on the accident date is a breach entitling the insurer to pay and recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Provides useful analysis of Section 15 of the MV Act on licence renewal and confirms that even a temporary gap in licence validity constitutes a breach.
supporting.quote: In the interregnum period i.e., from 30-04-2008 to 04-07-2008, the driver of offending Maruthi Omni was not holding valid and effective driving license and the accident had occurred on 2.7.2008.

adverse.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
adverse.principle: The insurer has a statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties even if there is a breach of policy conditions (such as an invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover the same from the insured.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will cite this to argue that the insurer MUST pay the full compensation to the claimants first, regardless of the licence breach. They will say the insurer's only remedy is to recover from the owner afterwards — not to avoid payment.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This does not defeat our defence — it confirms the 'pay and recover' framework. Our position is not that we should pay nothing, but that we should not bear the ultimate liability. We can distinguish by arguing that the breach here (no licence at all) is a 'fundamental breach' that goes to the root of the contract, and we accept the pay-and-recover outcome.
adverse.quote: The insurer has a statutory liability to pay the compensation to the third party and will simply have the right to recover the same from the insured/tortfeasor either in the same proceedings or by independent proceedings.

adverse.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
adverse.principle: An insurer cannot disown its liability to third parties on the ground that the driver, while possessing a valid LMV licence, lacked an endorsement to drive the vehicle as a commercial vehicle.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will cite this Supreme Court judgment to argue that even licence deficiencies do not allow the insurer to escape third-party liability. They will try to extend its reasoning to 'no licence' cases.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is distinguishable on facts: the driver there HAD a valid LMV licence — the dispute was only about the absence of a commercial endorsement. In our case, the driver had NO licence at all. The Supreme Court itself noted that the driver 'was holding a valid driving licence to drive light motor vehicle.' The ratio is expressly limited to cases where the driver holds some licence. Where there is no licence at all, the breach is fundamental.
adverse.quote: In the instant case, admittedly the driver was holding a valid driving licence to drive light motor vehicle. There is no dispute that the motor vehicle in question, by which accident took place, was Mahindra Maxi Cab.

adverse.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
adverse.principle: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy an award obtained by a third party regardless of policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will cite this to argue that even a completely invalid licence (expired = no valid licence) does not absolve the insurer of liability to the third party. They will say the insurer must pay first.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case actually supports the pay-and-recover framework we accept. The court held the insurer liable to the third party but did not say the insurer bore the ultimate loss. Moreover, the case involved an expired licence that was subsequently renewed — not a case where the driver never held a licence at all. Our case is stronger on the facts.
adverse.quote: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy an award obtained by a third party under the Motor Vehicles Act regardless of any policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence.

adverse.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
adverse.principle: In third-party claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific heavy vehicle class, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover from the insured.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will cite this for the broad proposition that the insurer must always pay third parties first, regardless of licence defects. They will argue that the 'pay and recover' principle is the ceiling of what the insurer can get.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Again, this case is about a driver who held an LMV licence with a transport endorsement but lacked the specific endorsement for a heavy goods vehicle — not a case of no licence at all. The court itself relied on Swaran Singh and Iyyapan, which both involved drivers who held some form of licence. Where the driver has no licence whatsoever, the breach is more fundamental.
adverse.quote: The Hon'ble Supreme Court has consistently held that in case of Third Party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so directed, to recover the same from the insured.

adverse.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. Thr. ... vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
adverse.principle: Even if the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer remains liable to satisfy third-party claims subject to a right of recovery from the vehicle owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: This is a case where our own company (National Insurance) was directed to pay and recover. The opposing side will use this against us to argue that National Insurance itself has accepted this position in other cases.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The case actually confirms the pay-and-recover framework we are prepared to accept. It does not hold that the insurer bears the ultimate liability. We can argue that this is precisely the remedy we seek — pay to the claimants, recover from the owner. The case also involved a tanker (hazardous goods), which has additional regulatory requirements, making it distinguishable.
adverse.quote: Even if the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer remains liable to satisfy third-party claims subject to a right of recovery from the vehicle owner.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
adverse.principle: For driving a goods carriage vehicle carrying dangerous/hazardous goods, a special endorsement is mandatory; absence thereof constitutes a breach entitling the insurer to pay and recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: If the truck was carrying hazardous goods, the opposing side might argue that the driver's lack of a special endorsement is a separate issue from having no licence at all, and that the insurer must still pay.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case actually supports the insurer's position — it confirms that a licence defect (missing special endorsement) is a breach, and the insurer gets pay-and-recover. It does not cut against us.
adverse.quote: The insurance company cannot escape its liability to make payment of compensation awarded in favour of the claimants. Once the payment is made, the insurance company has right to recover the same from the insured.

adverse.title: Kamal S/O Shiv Ram vs Mursleem S/O Mohd. Akil
adverse.principle: Driving without a valid licence can constitute contributory negligence, reducing the compensation payable.
adverse.risk_to_client: This case is about the injured claimant himself driving without a licence (contributory negligence by the claimant), not about the tortfeasor's driver lacking a licence. It is in a different factual context.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is about contributory negligence of the claimant, not about the insurer's defence against a third-party claim. It does not apply to our facts where the deceased was not the driver but a third party hit by our insured's truck.
adverse.quote: The contributory negligence of injured is proved in view of testimony of PW-1 Kamal who categorically deposed ... he did not have DL at the time of accident.

priority_arguments: 1. Fundamental breach: Driving a truck without any driving licence is a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy under Section 149(2)(a)(ii) of the MV Act. Cite doc_024 (Sunil Shreesail Killiket) which expressly holds that 'driving a motor vehicle without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach' and that the insurer is 'absolved from its liability' to the insured.

2. Burden of proof discharged: The insurer can discharge its burden by (a) examining an RTO official to confirm no licence was issued, (b) relying on the charge sheet which alleges no licence, and (c) the owner's failure to produce the driver's licence despite opportunity. Cite doc_035 (V.Vijayakumar) for the template of proving breach through RTO evidence, and doc_025 (Yallavva) for the burden-of-proof framework.

3. Pay and recover is the correct remedy: Even after proving breach, the insurer must pay the third-party claimants but is entitled to recover from the insured owner. This is the consistent position across all mixed-outcome judgments. Cite doc_033 (Satto), doc_024, doc_025, doc_027.

4. No licence at all is worse than wrong class/expired: Distinguish S.Iyyapan (doc_032) and Chennamma (doc_027) on the ground that those cases involved drivers who held some form of licence — our driver had none. The breach is more fundamental.

5. The owner's negligence in permitting an unlicensed driver: Under Swaran Singh principles (as cited in doc_025), the insurer must prove the insured was negligent in permitting the unlicensed driver. The owner's failure to produce the licence and the charge sheet alleging no licence are strong evidence of this.
strategy.compensation_range: Cannot estimate without knowing the deceased's age, income, and number of dependents. The quantum will be computed under the Sarla Verma / Pranay Sethi framework. The insurer's exposure is the full award amount, but with a right to recover the entire sum from the insured owner.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: The compensation will be computed by the Tribunal under Section 166 of the MV Act using the multiplier method. The insurer's liability is to pay the award in the first instance, with liberty to recover from the owner. The insurer should not resist quantum (which is the claimants' entitlement) but should focus on establishing the breach and securing the pay-and-recover order.
risks: 1. The Tribunal may hold that the insurer failed to discharge its burden of proving the breach — if the owner produces a licence or the charge sheet is ambiguous. The insurer must lead independent evidence (RTO records, RW examination).

2. The Tribunal may treat the absence of a licence as a 'minor breach' if the driver had some driving experience or if the owner can show reasonable belief that the driver was licensed. This is a factual risk.

3. The claimants may argue that the insurer is liable without any right of recovery if the policy is a 'Act only' policy — though doc_025 (Yallavva FB) holds that pay-and-recover applies regardless of policy type.

4. If the deceased was a high-income earner, the quantum could be very large, making the recovery from the owner practically difficult. The insurer should seek a direction for recovery in the same proceedings, not by separate suit.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal under Section 166 MV Act. The primary relief sought should be: (a) a declaration that the driver had no valid licence, constituting a fundamental breach; (b) an order directing the insurer to pay the compensation to the claimants in the first instance; (c) a concomitant order granting the insurer the right to recover the entire awarded amount from the insured owner, enforceable in the same proceedings.

caveats: 1. No judgment in this corpus holds that an insurer can completely avoid paying third-party compensation when the driver had no licence. Every single licence-defect case in the corpus (14 judgments) either orders pay-and-recover or holds the insurer directly liable. The insurer should not expect to walk away without paying.
2. The criminal cases (doc_016, doc_017) are about criminal negligence, not civil compensation. They are not directly relevant to the claim proceedings.
3. doc_005 (L And T Insurance Co Ltd vs Bindudevi Samharu Yadav) concerns the Section 167 bar and Workmen's Compensation Act — it is in a different area of law and should not be cited.

4. doc_031 (Laxmi Narain Dhut) is the only judgment that expressly 'favours insurer' but it primarily concerns the distinction between third-party and own-damage claims. It does not give the insurer a right to refuse payment to third parties.

5. The corpus does not contain any judgment where the insurer was completely exonerated from paying third-party compensation on the ground of the driver having no licence. The consistent position across all relevant judgments is that the insurer must pay the third party and then recover from the insured.

args.question: We represent National Insurance Co. The deceased's family claims compensation for a death caused by our insured's truck, whose driver had no valid driving licence. What precedents support our defence, and what authorities cut against us?

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving a motor vehicle without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy, absolving the insurer of direct liability to indemnify the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had no driving licence at all on the date of accident — directly on point with our facts where the truck driver had no valid licence.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest authority for establishing that the licence defect is a 'fundamental breach' — not a minor or inconsequential deviation. The tribunal expressly held the insurer 'not liable to pay the compensation' and 'absolved from its liability' to the insured, though it ordered pay-and-recover for the third party.
supporting.quote: Hence, it is held that as rightly argued by the learned counsel for the respondent No.2 the respondent No.1 has breached the fundamental condition of the policy by allowing the driver who has no driving licence to drive the vehicle. ... the respondent No.2 is not liable to pay the compensation and he is absolved from its liability.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: The insurer bears the initial burden of proving the breach under Section 149(2). Once proved, the insurer must still satisfy the third-party award but is entitled to recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: This Full Bench decision clarifies the burden of proof framework: the insurer must prove the breach (no valid licence) and the insured's negligence in permitting the unlicensed driver. Our case aligns because we can prove the driver had no licence.
supporting.why_it_matters: Provides the complete legal framework: (a) burden on insurer to prove breach, (b) even after proving breach, pay third party, (c) recover from insured. It also cites Swaran Singh's principles on what constitutes a fundamental breach.
supporting.quote: Even if there is any violation or breach of condition of a policy, the insurer has to discharge the initial burden of proving the grounds taken under Section 149(2) of the Act. In spite of that, the insurer has to indemnify the amount and can recover the same from the insured.

supporting.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
supporting.principle: The Swaran Singh principles apply exclusively to third-party risks and have no application to own-damage claims. A fake licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
supporting.fact_alignment: While this case is about fake licences and own-damage claims, it confirms that the Swaran Singh framework (which limits insurer defences) is confined to third-party claims — which our case is. It also confirms that where the licence is fundamentally invalid, the insurer's position is stronger.
supporting.why_it_matters: This Supreme Court judgment is the only one in the corpus that expressly favours the insurer. It clarifies that the 'pay and recover' principle applies to third-party claims (which is our case) and that the insurer's right to recover is well-established.
supporting.quote: In view of the above analysis the following situations emerge: 1. The decision in Swaran Singh's case (supra) has no application to cases other than third party risks. ... 3. supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver holds only an LMV licence but drives a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions, and the insurer is entitled to pay and recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: Our case involves a truck (goods carriage/transport vehicle). If the driver had no licence at all (not merely the wrong class), this case is less directly on point, but it supports the principle that driving without the proper authorisation is a breach.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar W/O Late ...

supporting.fact_alignment: While our case involves no licence at all (not an expired one), this case supports the broader principle that absence of a valid licence on the accident date is a breach entitling the insurer to pay and recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Provides useful analysis of Section 15 of the MV Act on licence renewal and confirms that even a temporary gap in licence validity constitutes a breach.
supporting.quote: In the interregnum period i.e., from 30-04-2008 to 04-07-2008, the driver of offending Maruthi Omni was not holding valid and effective driving license and the accident had occurred on 2.7.2008.

adverse.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
adverse.principle: The insurer has a statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties even if there is a breach of policy conditions (such as an invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover the same from the insured.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will cite this to argue that the insurer MUST pay the full compensation to the claimants first, regardless of the licence breach. They will say the insurer's only remedy is to recover from the owner afterwards — not to avoid payment.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This does not defeat our defence — it confirms the 'pay and recover' framework. Our position is not that we should pay nothing, but that we should not bear the ultimate liability. We can distinguish by arguing that the breach here (no licence at all) is a 'fundamental breach' that goes to the root of the contract, and we accept the pay-and-recover outcome.
adverse.quote: The insurer has a statutory liability to pay the compensation to the third party and will simply have the right to recover the same from the insured/tortfeasor either in the same proceedings or by independent proceedings.

adverse.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. Thr. ... vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
adverse.principle: Even if the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer remains liable to satisfy third-party claims subject to a right of recovery from the vehicle owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: This is a case where our own company (National Insurance) was directed to pay and recover. The opposing side will use this against us to argue that National Insurance itself has accepted this position in other cases — that even with no valid licence, the insurer must pay first.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The case actually confirms the pay-and-recover framework we are prepared to accept. It does not hold that the insurer bears the ultimate liability. We can argue that this is precisely the remedy we seek — pay to the claimants, recover from the owner. The case also involved a tanker (hazardous goods), which has additional regulatory requirements, making it distinguishable on facts.
adverse.quote: Even if the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer remains liable to satisfy third-party claims subject to a right of recovery from the vehicle owner.

adverse.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
adverse.principle: An insurer cannot disown its liability to third parties on the ground that the driver, while possessing a valid LMV licence, lacked an endorsement to drive the vehicle as a commercial vehicle.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will cite this Supreme Court judgment to argue that even licence deficiencies do not allow the insurer to escape third-party liability. They will try to extend its reasoning to 'no licence' cases, arguing that the Supreme Court has taken a liberal approach to licence defects.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is distinguishable on facts: the driver there HAD a valid LMV licence — the dispute was only about the absence of a commercial endorsement. In our case, the driver had NO licence at all. The Supreme Court itself noted that the driver 'was holding a valid driving licence to drive light motor vehicle.' The ratio is expressly limited to cases where the driver holds some licence. Where there is no licence at all, the breach is fundamental.
adverse.quote: In the instant case, admittedly the driver was holding a valid driving licence to drive light motor vehicle. There is no dispute that the motor vehicle in question, by which accident took place, was Mahindra Maxi Cab.

adverse.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
adverse.principle: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy an award obtained by a third party regardless of policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will cite this to argue that even a completely invalid licence (expired = no valid licence) does not absolve the insurer of liability to the third party. They will say the insurer must pay first.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case actually supports the pay-and-recover framework we accept. The court held the insurer liable to the third party but did not say the insurer bore the ultimate loss. Moreover, the case involved an expired licence that was subsequently renewed — not a case where the driver never held a licence at all. Our case is stronger on the facts because the driver never had any licence.
adverse.quote: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy an award obtained by a third party under the Motor Vehicles Act regardless of any policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence.

adverse.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
adverse.principle: In third-party claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific heavy vehicle class, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover from the insured.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will cite this for the broad proposition that the insurer must always pay third parties first, regardless of licence defects. They will argue that the 'pay and recover' principle is the ceiling of what the insurer can get.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Again, this case is about a driver who held an LMV licence with a transport endorsement but lacked the specific endorsement for a heavy goods vehicle — not a case of no licence at all. The court itself relied on Swaran Singh and Iyyapan, which both involved drivers who held some form of licence. Where the driver has no licence whatsoever, the breach is more fundamental.
adverse.quote: The Hon'ble Supreme Court has consistently held that in case of Third Party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so directed, to recover the same from the insured.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
adverse.principle: For driving a goods carriage vehicle carrying dangerous/hazardous goods, a special endorsement is mandatory; absence thereof constitutes a breach entitling the insurer to pay and recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: If the truck was carrying hazardous goods, the opposing side might argue that the driver's lack of a special endorsement is a separate issue from having no licence at all, and that the insurer must still pay. However, this case actually supports the insurer's position overall.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case actually supports the insurer's position — it confirms that a licence defect (missing special endorsement) is a breach, and the insurer gets pay-and-recover. It does not cut against us. The only risk is if the claimants try to argue that the insurer should have raised this specific ground, but our ground (no licence at all) is broader and stronger.
adverse.quote: The insurance company cannot escape its liability to make payment of compensation awarded in favour of the claimants. Once the payment is made, the insurance company has right to recover the same from the insured.

priority_arguments: 1. Fundamental breach: Driving a truck without any driving licence is a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy under Section 149(2)(a)(ii) of the MV Act. Cite doc_024 (Sunil Shreesail Killiket) which expressly holds that 'driving a motor vehicle without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach' and that the insurer is 'absolved from its liability' to the insured.

2. Burden of proof discharged: The insurer can discharge its burden by (a) examining an RTO official to confirm no licence was issued, (b) relying on the charge sheet which alleges no licence, and (c) the owner's failure to produce the driver's licence despite opportunity. Cite doc_035 (V.Vijayakumar) for the template of proving breach through RTO evidence, and doc_025 (Yallavva) for the burden-of-proof framework.

3. Pay and recover is the correct remedy: Even after proving breach, the insurer must pay the third-party claimants but is entitled to recover from the insured owner. This is the consistent position across all mixed-outcome judgments. Cite doc_033 (Satto), doc_024, doc_025, doc_027.

4. No licence at all is worse than wrong class/expired: Distinguish S.Iyyapan (doc_032) and Chennamma (doc_027) on the ground that those cases involved drivers who held some form of licence — our driver had none. The breach is more fundamental.

5. The owner's negligence in permitting an unlicensed driver: Under Swaran Singh principles (as cited in doc_025), the insurer must prove the insured was negligent in permitting the unlicensed driver. The owner's failure to produce the licence and the charge sheet alleging no licence are strong evidence of this.
strategy.compensation_range: Cannot estimate without knowing the deceased's age, income, and number of dependents. The quantum will be computed under the Sarla Verma / Pranay Sethi framework. The insurer's exposure is the full award amount, but with a right to recover the entire sum from the insured owner.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: The compensation will be computed by the Tribunal under Section 166 of the MV Act using the multiplier method. The insurer's liability is to pay the award in the first instance, with liberty to recover from the owner. The insurer should not resist quantum (which is the claimants' entitlement) but should focus on establishing the breach and securing the pay-and-recover order.
risks: 1. The Tribunal may hold that the insurer failed to discharge its burden of proving the breach — if the owner produces a licence or the charge sheet is ambiguous. The insurer must lead independent evidence (RTO records, RW examination).

2. The Tribunal may treat the absence of a licence as a 'minor breach' if the driver had some driving experience or if the owner can show reasonable belief that the driver was licensed. This is a factual risk.

3. The claimants may argue that the insurer is liable without any right of recovery if the policy is an 'Act only' policy — though doc_025 (Yallavva FB) holds that pay-and-recover applies regardless of policy type.

4. If the deceased was a high-income earner, the quantum could be very large, making the recovery from the owner practically difficult. The insurer should seek a direction for recovery in the same proceedings, not by separate suit.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal under Section 166 MV Act. The primary relief sought should be: (a) a declaration that the driver had no valid licence, constituting a fundamental breach; (b) an order directing the insurer to pay the compensation to the claimants in the first instance; (c) a concomitant order granting the insurer the right to recover the entire awarded amount from the insured owner, enforceable in the same proceedings.

caveats: 1. No judgment in this corpus holds that an insurer can completely avoid paying third-party compensation when the driver had no licence. Every single licence-defect case in the corpus (14 judgments) either orders pay-and-recover or holds the insurer directly liable. The insurer should not expect to walk away without paying.

2. doc_028 (United India Insurance Co. Ltd. vs Sukumarbai Suryakant Nikam) — This judgment exonerated the insurer completely, but on an entirely different ground: the claimant was a passenger in a private vehicle for hire/reward, who was held NOT to be a 'third party' under Section 147. This case is about the scope of third-party coverage, not about licence defects. It has no application to our facts where the deceased was a third-party road user hit by our insured's truck. The opposing side has no reason to cite it.

3. doc_030 (Dadapeera vs Mallesh) — This judgment exonerated the insurer because the claimant was travelling on a tractor's mud-guard in violation of Regulation 28, and was therefore not a 'third party' entitled to the benefit of pay-and-recover. This is about the scope of statutory coverage for unauthorised passengers on agricultural vehicles, not about licence defects. It has no application to our facts where the deceased was a third-party road user. The opposing side has no reason to cite it.
4. The criminal cases (doc_016, doc_017) are about criminal negligence under the IPC, not civil compensation under the MV Act. They are not directly relevant to the claim proceedings.
5. doc_005 (L And T Insurance Co Ltd vs Bindudevi Samharu Yadav) concerns the Section 167 bar and Workmen's Compensation Act — it is in a different area of law and should not be cited.

6. doc_009 (Kamal vs Mursleem) is about contributory negligence of the injured claimant himself (who was driving without a licence), not about the insurer's defence against a third-party claim. It does not apply to our facts.

adverse.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
adverse.principle: An insurer cannot disown its liability to third parties on the ground that the driver, while possessing a valid LMV licence, lacked an endorsement to drive the vehicle as a commercial vehicle.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will cite this Supreme Court judgment to argue that even licence deficiencies do not allow the insurer to escape third-party liability. They will try to extend its reasoning to 'no licence' cases, arguing that the Supreme Court has taken a liberal approach to licence defects.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is distinguishable on facts: the driver there HAD a valid LMV licence — the dispute was only about the absence of a commercial endorsement. In our case, the driver had NO licence at all. The Supreme Court itself noted that the driver 'was holding a valid driving licence to drive light motor vehicle.' The ratio is expressly limited to cases where the driver holds some licence. Where there is no licence at all, the breach is fundamental.
adverse.quote: In the instant case, admittedly the driver was holding a valid driving licence to drive light motor vehicle. There is no dispute that the motor vehicle in question, by which accident took place, was Mahindra Maxi Cab.

adverse.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
adverse.principle: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy an award obtained by a third party regardless of policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will cite this to argue that even a completely invalid licence (expired = no valid licence) does not absolve the insurer of liability to the third party. They will say the insurer must pay first.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case actually supports the pay-and-recover framework we accept. The court held the insurer liable to the third party but did not say the insurer bore the ultimate loss. Moreover, the case involved an expired licence that was subsequently renewed — not a case where the driver never held a licence at all. Our case is stronger on the facts because the driver never had any licence.

adverse.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
adverse.principle: In third-party claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific heavy vehicle class, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover from the insured.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will cite this for the broad proposition that the insurer must always pay third parties first, regardless of licence defects. They will argue that the 'pay and recover' principle is the ceiling of what the insurer can get.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Again, this case is about a driver who held an LMV licence with a transport endorsement but lacked the specific endorsement for a heavy goods vehicle — not a case of no licence at all. The court itself relied on Swaran Singh and Iyyapan, which both involved drivers who held some form of licence. Where the driver has no licence whatsoever, the breach is more fundamental.
adverse.quote: The Hon'ble Supreme Court has consistently held that in case of Third Party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so directed, to recover the same from the insured.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
adverse.principle: For driving a goods carriage vehicle carrying dangerous/hazardous goods, a special endorsement is mandatory; absence thereof constitutes a breach entitling the insurer to pay and recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: If the truck was carrying hazardous goods, the opposing side might argue that the driver's lack of a special endorsement is a separate issue from having no licence at all, and that the insurer must still pay. However, this case actually supports the insurer's position overall.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case actually supports the insurer's position — it confirms that a licence defect (missing special endorsement) is a breach, and the insurer gets pay-and-recover. It does not cut against us. The only risk is if the claimants try to argue that the insurer should have raised this specific ground, but our ground (no licence at all) is broader and stronger.
adverse.quote: The insurance company cannot escape its liability to make payment of compensation awarded in favour of the claimants. Once the payment is made, the insurance company has right to recover the same from the insured.

priority_arguments: 1. Fundamental breach: Driving a truck without any driving licence is a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy under Section 149(2)(a)(ii) of the MV Act. Cite doc_024 (Sunil Shreesail Killiket) which expressly holds that 'driving a motor vehicle without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach' and that the insurer is 'absolved from its liability' to the insured.

2. Burden of proof discharged: The insurer can discharge its burden by (a) examining an RTO official to confirm no licence was issued, (b) relying on the charge sheet which alleges no licence, and (c) the owner's failure to produce the driver's licence despite opportunity. Cite doc_035 (V.Vijayakumar) for the template of proving breach through RTO evidence, and doc_025 (Yallavva) for the burden-of-proof framework.

3. Pay and recover is the correct remedy: Even after proving breach, the insurer must pay the third-party claimants but is entitled to recover from the insured owner. This is the consistent position across all mixed-outcome judgments. Cite doc_033 (Satto), doc_024, doc_025, doc_027.

4. No licence at all is worse than wrong class/expired: Distinguish S.Iyyapan (doc_032) and Chennamma (doc_027) on the ground that those cases involved drivers who held some form of licence — our driver had none. The breach is more fundamental.

5. The owner's negligence in permitting an unlicensed driver: Under Swaran Singh principles (as cited in doc_025), the insurer must prove the insured was negligent in permitting the unlicensed driver. The owner's failure to produce the licence and the charge sheet alleging no licence are strong evidence of this.
strategy.compensation_range: Cannot estimate without knowing the deceased's age, income, and number of dependents. The quantum will be computed under the Sarla Verma / Pranay Sethi framework. The insurer's exposure is the full award amount, but with a right to recover the entire sum from the insured owner.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: The compensation will be computed by the Tribunal under Section 166 of the MV Act using the multiplier method. The insurer's liability is to pay the award in the first instance, with liberty to recover from the owner. The insurer should not resist quantum (which is the claimants' entitlement) but should focus on establishing the breach and securing the pay-and-recover order.
risks: 1. The Tribunal may hold that the insurer failed to discharge its burden of proving the breach — if the owner produces a licence or the charge sheet is ambiguous. The insurer must lead independent evidence (RTO records, RW examination).

2. The Tribunal may treat the absence of a licence as a 'minor breach' if the driver had some driving experience or if the owner can show reasonable belief that the driver was licensed. This is a factual risk.

3. The claimants may argue that the insurer is liable without any right of recovery if the policy is an 'Act only' policy — though doc_025 (Yallavva FB) holds that pay-and-recover applies regardless of policy type.

4. If the deceased was a high-income earner, the quantum could be very large, making the recovery from the owner practically difficult. The insurer should seek a direction for recovery in the same proceedings, not by separate suit.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal under Section 166 MV Act. The primary relief sought should be: (a) a declaration that the driver had no valid licence, constituting a fundamental breach; (b) an order directing the insurer to pay the compensation to the claimants in the first instance; (c) a concomitant order granting the insurer the right to recover the entire awarded amount from the insured owner, enforceable in the same proceedings.

caveats: 1. No judgment in this corpus holds that an insurer can completely avoid paying third-party compensation when the driver had no licence. Every single licence-defect case in the corpus (14 judgments) either orders pay-and-recover or holds the insurer directly liable. The insurer should not expect to walk away without paying.

2. doc_028 (United India Insurance Co. Ltd. vs Sukumarbai Suryakant Nikam) — This judgment exonerated the insurer completely, but on an entirely different ground: the claimant was a passenger in a private vehicle for hire/reward, who was held NOT to be a 'third party' under Section 147. This case is about the scope of third-party coverage, not about licence defects. It has no application to our facts where the deceased was a third-party road user hit by our insured's truck. The opposing side has no reason to cite it.

3. doc_030 (Dadapeera vs Mallesh) — This judgment exonerated the insurer because the claimant was travelling on a tractor's mud-guard in violation of Regulation 28, and was therefore not a 'third party' entitled to the benefit of pay-and-recover. This is about the scope of statutory coverage for unauthorised passengers on agricultural vehicles, not about licence defects. It has no application to our facts where the deceased was a third-party road user. The opposing side has no reason to cite it.
4. The criminal cases (doc_016, doc_017) are about criminal negligence under the IPC, not civil compensation under the MV Act. They are not directly relevant to the claim proceedings.
5. doc_005 (L And T Insurance Co Ltd vs Bindudevi Samharu Yadav) concerns the Section 167 bar and Workmen's Compensation Act — it is in a different area of law and should not be cited.

6. doc_009 (Kamal vs Mursleem) is about contributory negligence of the injured claimant himself (who was driving without a licence), not about the insurer's defence against a third-party claim. It does not apply to our facts.
